title: Chevalley constructibility and open pieces of constructible sets
statement:
Let $k$ be a field. Use affine schemes and spectra as in [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-affine-spectrum], finite type over $k$ as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and constructible subsets as in [def-weil-constructible-subset].

1. (Chevalley.) If $f:X\to Y$ is a morphism over $k$ of affine schemes of
   finite type over $k$, then the image of every constructible subset of
   $X$ is a constructible subset of $Y$. In particular $f(X)$ is
   constructible.
2. If $S$ is a nonempty constructible subset of an affine scheme $Y$ of
   finite type over $k$, then $S$ contains a nonempty open subset of its
   closure $\overline S$. In particular, a nonempty dense constructible subset of
   $Y$ contains a nonempty open subset of $Y$.

proof.text: First let $Y$ be any affine scheme of finite type over $k$, with structure morphism $p:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Apply the definition of finite type to $p$ and the affine open $\operatorname{Spec}k$ of $\operatorname{Spec}k$: $Y$ has an affine open cover by spectra $\operatorname{Spec}A_j$ of finitely generated $k$-algebras $A_j$. The Noetherianity node makes each $A_j$ Noetherian, so $Y$ is locally Noetherian by definition. The affine-scheme node makes $Y$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated; in particular $Y$ is a Noetherian scheme (locally Noetherian and quasi-compact). Now let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism over $k$ as in (1), so that the structure morphism $q$ of $X$ equals $p\circ f$. Apply clause (a) of the finite-type cancellation node to $X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{p}\operatorname{Spec}k$: the composite $q$ is locally of finite type by hypothesis, so $f$ is locally of finite type. The locally Noetherian finite-presentation node now makes $f$ locally of finite presentation. Since $X$ and $Y$ are affine, $f$ is affine by the morphism-of-affine-schemes node and hence quasi-compact by clause (3) of the affine-morphism node.

proof.text: For (2), use the definition of constructibility to write $S=\bigcup_{i=1}^r S_i$ with $S_i=U_i\cap F_i$, $U_i$ open and $F_i$ closed in $Y$, discarding empty pieces. Since $S\ne\varnothing$, $r>0$. Set $Z=\overline S$. Closure commutes with finite unions, so $Z=\bigcup_i\overline{S_i}$. The closed-subset component node applies to $Y$, which is a Noetherian scheme by the first paragraph of step 1, and the closed subset $Z$: write $Z=C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_t$ as its finitely many distinct irreducible components. Here $t>0$ since $Z$ contains $S\ne\varnothing$. Each $C_j$ is closed in $Z$, and therefore in $Y$.

source.place: paragraph (2), finite locally closed decomposition and finite irreducible components of Z; Stacks 005G (definition-constructible), 0BA8 (properties-lemma-Noetherian-irreducible-components)

proof.text: We will use the finite closed-cover consequence of the definition of irreducibility. If an irreducible nonempty subspace $C$ is contained in $D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_r$ with all $D_i$ closed, then $C=\bigcup_i(C\cap D_i)$; induction on $r$ using the binary closed-union definition shows $C\subseteq D_i$ for some $i$ (the case $r=0$ is excluded by nonemptiness). Apply this with $C=C_1$ and $D_i=\overline{S_i}$ to choose $i$ with $C_1\subseteq\overline{S_i}$.

source.place: paragraph (2), finite closed cover of the chosen component; induction from Stacks 004V (definition-irreducible-components)

proof.text: Let $\Omega=Z\setminus\bigcup_{j=2}^t C_j$. This is open in $Z$ and contained in $C_1$, since the components cover $Z$. It is nonempty: otherwise $C_1\subseteq\bigcup_{j=2}^t C_j$, and the finite closed-cover argument of step 4 would put $C_1$ inside one distinct component $C_j$, contradicting maximality in the definition of irreducible components. For $t=1$ the union removed is empty and $\Omega=Z\ne\varnothing$.

source.place: paragraph (2), complement of the remaining components; maximality and the finite closed-cover argument

proof.text: Choose an open subset $O\subseteq Y$ with $\Omega=O\cap Z$, by the subspace topology. Since $\overline{S_i}\subseteq Z$, we have $O\cap\overline{S_i}=\Omega\cap\overline{S_i}=\Omega$, the last equality following from $\Omega\subseteq C_1\subseteq\overline{S_i}$. Thus $\Omega$ is a nonempty open subset of $\overline{S_i}$ and meets its dense subset $S_i$. Also $S_i\subseteq F_i$ and $F_i$ is closed, so $\overline{S_i}\subseteq F_i$ and $S_i=U_i\cap\overline{S_i}$. Consequently $S_i\cap\Omega=U_i\cap\Omega$ is nonempty, open in $Z$, and contained in $S$. This proves (2). If $S$ is also dense in $Y$, then $Z=Y$, giving the final assertion under the same nonemptiness hypothesis.
